quote: Usually, a Jew would somehow just-not-think-about the logical implication that God had permitted a tragedy.
content: The blessing is a fair correction to the general statement: Baruch dayan ha-emet assigns every death to divine judgment. What surprised the essay was something more specific: a spontaneous, unscripted narrative in which God dismantled a mother strategically, "her memory, and her speech, and then finally her smile." A formula recited at the graveside is one thing, and dwelling on the design of a slow cruelty is another, and the essay's prediction concerned the second. That prediction came true. Job, tzadik ve-ra lo and Guide III:17–18 also fit the essay's model rather than refuting it. The essay says the tradition is "allowed to notice inconsistencies and contradictions, but only for purposes of explaining them away," and a large theodicy literature is what that looks like.

quote: You don’t even ask whether the incident reflects poorly on God, so there’s no need to quickly blurt out “The ways of God are mysterious!”
content: The essay says the old rabbis asked. It credits them with seeing "the harshness of the Plagues," gives the ten drops of wine as its example, and then adds the qualification that answers Fable in advance: "sympathetic to the suffering of the Egyptians, but not so sympathetic that you stand up and say, 'This is not right!'" Megillah 10b fits that sentence exactly. God silences the angels' song, and the drowning goes ahead; the midrash grieves for the victims without asking whether the act was right. The essay's "you" is the modern practitioner doubting in private, not the Talmud, and its claim is that the grief has been made into a ritual that stops short of the moral question. The sources Fable cites show the ritual.

quote: The reason that educated religious people stay religious, I suspect, is that when they doubt, they are subconsciously very careful to attack their own beliefs only at the strongest points
content: Social variables predict who comes to doubt. The essay's question starts after that: given an educated believer who does doubt, which objections do they pick? On that, the selective-exposure evidence is direct. Across 91 studies, people prefer information that confirms their attitudes, and the preference is strongest when commitment to the attitude is high, which describes a believer questioning a lifelong faith (Hart et al. 2009). The Gervais & Norenzayan replication failure is well taken, but the essay never relied on priming analytic thought. Its claim is that doubting is steered away from the painful objections. The grand-uncle's reasons for leaving go unreported, but his own words at the funeral did face the painful objection the essay says believers avoid.

quote: Punch yourself in the solar plexus. Stick a knife in your heart, and wiggle to widen the hole.
content: The essay includes a structured procedure, in the sentence before the imagery: "Ask yourself what smart people who disagree would say to your first reply, and your second reply." That is consider-the-opposite applied twice, together with an instruction not to "rehearse standard objections whose standard counters would make you feel better." Rumination is repetitive, passive focus on one's own distress. The essay's instruction is to evaluate the objection one has been avoiding, which is closer to exposure than to rumination. The clinical literature points the same way. Experiential avoidance, the habitual flinch away from painful content, predicts worse outcomes across disorders (Hayes et al. 1996). The Gendlin lines are an exposure script, and exposure is one of psychotherapy's best-supported methods.
